$$
y_p = x (\alpha \cos{2x} + \beta \sin{2x}),
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x), \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ -4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = -1$ and $\beta = 0.$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) = -x \cos{2x},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-9012ef7a-2685-5e88-afc5-3c045fe01d15" :question/id #uuid "9012ef7a-2685-5e88-afc5-3c045fe01d15" :question/math-academy-id "q-64273" :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

"Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=0
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1\pm 2\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(4\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4\alpha +2\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ -2\alpha +4\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-73960a55-87e7-51f7-88d8-3235589147ec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =2$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {y}^{″} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

$$
A+B-1=0.

$$

$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
-A+2B=-1.
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -A+2B=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,$ $B=0.$
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088955 :tutorial/content "Let's solve the following second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing:

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088951 :tutorial/content "Given a second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing $f(x) = a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x,$ if $\cos \omega x$ or $\sin \omega x$ *is* a term in the complementary solution, then $a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x$ *cannot* be a particular solution. $$

$$

$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

$$

$$

$$

$$
-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x.

$$

$$

$$

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

$$

$$

$$

:question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =2$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {y}^{″} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B-1=0.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+2B{e}^{2x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
-A+2B=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -A+2B=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,$ $B=0.$
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351217 :question/id #uuid "77dcab2f-d394-5343-acb3-cfbabfe50eb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-8110"} {:db/id 17592186357575 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

In general, we say that a second-order ODE has **sinusoidal forcing** if $f(x)$ is a sinusoidal function of the form

$$
f(x) = a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x,
$$

where $\omega$ is a constant.

For example, the ODE below has sinusoidal forcing:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} - 2y= 2 \cos 2 x
$$

Solving a second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing is similar to the method for solving a second-order ODE with polynomial forcing. The general solution is still the sum of the complementary solution $y_c$ (i.e., the solution to the associated homogeneous ODE) and a particular solution $y_p\mathbin{:}$

$$
y = y_c + y_p
$$

The only difference is in how we find a particular solution. Given a second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing $f(x) = a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x,$ provided that $\sin \omega x$ and $\cos \omega x$ do not feature in the complementary solution, then we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p =\alpha \cos \omega x + \beta  \sin \omega x.
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are unknown constants to be determined." :tutorial/id #uuid "c922743e-1a32-51dd-a109-feac1b1930c5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4066 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "91f805b4-d536-567b-92f7-524437b74146" :step/math-academy-id 24264 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088661}} {:db/id 17592186088654 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087779 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087606 :question/id #uuid "c25573a9-f51a-5cf2-aa32-a343e96dd732" :question/math-academy-id "e-6612"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "17b31ef7-a3d0-5315-8dbd-e92eafcce17f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048289} {:db/id 17592186048391} {:db/id 17592186050392} {:db/id 17592186050433}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088224} {:db/id 17592186088393} {:db/id 17592186335695} {:db/id 17592186351232} {:db/id 17592186351238} {:db/id 17592186351241} {:db/id 17592186357573}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Second-Order Differential Equation Using Sinusoidal Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "fcefea54-b58a-521e-b82e-14299e2f316d" :step/math-academy-id 24265 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088655}} {:db/id 17592186088655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088951 :tutorial/content "Given a second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing $f(x) = a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x,$ if $\cos \omega x$ or $\sin \omega x$ *is* a term in the complementary solution, then $a \cos \omega x + b \sin \omega x$ *cannot* be a particular solution. Instead, we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p = x(\alpha \cos \omega x + \beta  \sin \omega x).
$$

For example, let's find the solution to the following ODE:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + y= 4 \cos x.
$$

First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i},\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = \textrm{i}$ or $\lambda =  -\textrm{i}.$ Consequently, the complimentary solution is

$$
y_c = A\cos x + B \sin x.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $4 \cos x$ and $\cos x$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p = x (\alpha \cos x + \beta \sin x),
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}x+\beta \operatorname{sin}x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}x+\beta \operatorname{cos}x), \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}x+\beta \operatorname{cos}x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}x-\beta \operatorname{sin}x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}x+\beta \operatorname{cos}x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}x-\beta \operatorname{sin}x)+x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}x+\beta \operatorname{sin}x) & =4\operatorname{cos}x \\ -2\alpha \operatorname{sin}x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}x & =4\operatorname{cos}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\beta =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}x) \\ -2\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 2.$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = 2x \sin{x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}x+B\operatorname{sin}x+2x\operatorname{sin}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "703ca0f2-aa95-5326-811b-83d5a458ccd0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4067 :tutorial/title "The Case When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution Have the Same Term"} :step/id #uuid "38062346-4103-5ff0-815d-26c1948b8d40" :step/math-academy-id 24266 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088656}} {:db/id 17592186088656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087780 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087607 :question/id #uuid "b11bf2d1-c79a-5308-bcda-109d217b14cb" :question/math-academy-id "e-6613"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1292269f-5e99-5354-924d-824238118a8d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088227} {:db/id 17592186088395} {:db/id 17592186335696} {:db/id 17592186335697} {:db/id 17592186357574} {:db/id 17592186404440} {:db/id 17592186404586}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Dependent"} :step/id #uuid "ecd022a7-62c1-51a9-8e53-2f732b860fdf" :step/math-academy-id 24267 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088663}} {:db/id 17592186088661 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088955 :tutorial/content "Let's solve the following second-order ODE with sinusoidal forcing:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} - 2y= 2 \cos 2 x
$$

First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation (or auxiliary equation) is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = 1$ or $\lambda = -2.$ Consequently, the complementary solution is

$$
y_c = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2 x}.
$$

$$
y_p =\alpha \cos 2x + \beta  \sin 2x
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}2x \\ \,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}2x-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}2x-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}2x) & =2\operatorname{cos}2x \\ (2\beta -6\alpha )\operatorname{cos}2x+(-6\beta -2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}2x & =2\operatorname{cos}2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\beta -6\alpha =2 \\ -6\beta -2\alpha =0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

From the second equation, it follows that

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y_c = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2 x}.
$$

$$
y_p =\alpha \cos 2x + \beta  \sin 2x
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}2x \\ \,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}2x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}2x-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}2x-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}2x) & =2\operatorname{cos}2x \\ (2\beta -6\alpha )\operatorname{cos}2x+(-6\beta -2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}2x & =2\operatorname{cos}2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\beta -6\alpha =2 \\ -6\beta -2\alpha =0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\alpha = -3(0.1) = -0.3.
$$

$$
y_p = - 0.3 \cos 2x + 0.1  \sin 2x,

Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.

The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
